text.p: Austria's marathon privatisation of blue-blooded bank Creditanstalt-Bankverein was hurled back to the starting line on Monday after Finance Minister Viktor Klima rejected the only firm bid as "unacceptable".
Klima turned down the sole bid by an Austro-Italian-German consortium around EA Generali because it fell short of the conditions laid down by the government in October 1995.
"I very much regret....that the offer put forward by the consortium on September 6 cannot be accepted," Klima said in a statement.

The government had envisaged selling its entire stake of around 19.9 million shares, in the process ensuring the protection of national interests and guaranteeing "the best possible price" for the government's stake, Klima said.
The government was also aiming to improve the structure of Austria's overcrowded banking sector.

Klima, desperate to use the proceeds from the sale to fill the government's empty coffers, said CA would now work with U.S. investment house J.P. Morgan, to update the memorandum J.P Morgan prepared last year and come up with a new procedure for privatisation within a few weeks.
The sale of the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt, former bankers to the Habsburg Empire, has turned into Austria's longest-running privatisation.

For the past six years, a bevy of suitors -- among them Allianz Holding of Germany and CS Holding of Switzerland -- has lost interest in the bank after what they felt was a bias against foreign ownership in Austria.
The government was left with just one interested party -- the EA-Generali consortium which also includes Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana.

"The consortium regrets that it was not able to fully meet the expectations of the finance ministry," EA Generali said in a statement, adding that its bid failed because it did not cover the entire stake.
EA-Generali reportedly offered cash for about half the government's 19.9 million shares and proposed to sell the rest in a secondary offering, possibly financed via a convertible bond issue.

But EA Generali said the consortium remained interested in Creditanstalt, which commands a strong presence on the emerging markets of central and eastern Europe, and cited "a particular wish to include savings bank Die Erste in mutual considerations over the privatisation of CA."

The consortium was thrown into disarray just hours before Klima's September 6 bid deadline expired when Die Erste, Austria's biggest savings bank, left the group after hectic negotiations with its partners failed to produce agreement on a joint bid.
Die Erste had proposed forming an alliance with CA but the plan's critics rejected the scheme, pointing out that CA dwarfed Die Erste.
